concepts.name: Explain and agree on an approach before coding
Test your own code before saying you're done
Stating time and space complexity correctly
The four axes of a coding-interview rubric

questions.prompt: Your peer gives you: "Return the k most frequent words in a list." What is the best first move, according to the Tech Interview Handbook's checklist?

choices.text: Start coding a heap solution straight away, since time is short
Ask the interviewer what time complexity they expect you to reach
Paraphrase it, then clarify the input: empty list, ties, case, size
Write the brute force immediately, so that something works early on

questions.explanation: When you receive the question, the checklist says to paraphrase it back, clarify assumptions and the input's range and format (empty input, duplicates, large values), work through a small example, and not jump into coding right away. Here ties and case sensitivity change the expected output, and input size decides whether a simple sort is fine.

sources.claim: The cheatsheet says on receiving a question to paraphrase it, clarify assumptions and the input's range and format (sorted, duplicates, empty), work a small example, and not jump into coding right away.

questions.prompt: The task is: "Find two numbers in `nums` that add up to `target`." Which clarifying question is most likely to change your algorithm?

choices.text: Can I return the answer as a tuple instead of a list?
Should the function have a docstring?
Is it OK if I write a helper function?
Is `nums` sorted?

questions.explanation: If the array is sorted, two pointers moving in from both ends solve it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. If not, a hash map of seen values gives O(n) time and O(n) space. The other questions are about presentation. They are fine to ask, but they don't change the solution, and the checklist's clarifying questions target the input itself: its format, range and properties such as being sorted.

sources.claim: The cheatsheet's clarifying questions ask about input properties such as whether the input is sorted or has duplicates.

questions.prompt: You can see an O(n²) brute force and suspect an O(n) solution. What should you do next, according to the checklist?

choices.text: Explain both approaches with their time and space complexity, agree on one, then code
Code the O(n) solution straight away and explain it once it works
Code the brute force in full first, then rewrite it into the fast version
Think silently until you are sure of the O(n) solution

questions.explanation: Before coding, the checklist says to explain several approaches at a high level with their trade-offs, state the time and space complexity, and agree on the best approach with the interviewer. It warns against coding before the interviewer is on board. Silence hides the problem solving the interviewer is there to score, and a full brute force uses time you'll need for the better solution.

sources.title: Coding interview cheatsheet: Best practices before, during and after | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The cheatsheet says to explain a few approaches at a high level with trade-offs, state time and space complexity, agree on the best approach, and only code after the interviewer's green light.

questions.prompt: Your peer's written feedback says: "Started coding before I knew your plan." Describe what the first ten minutes of your next coding mock should look like.

model_answer.summary: Restate the problem and clarify the input, work a small example, then talk through one or two approaches with their complexity. Agree on one before writing any code, and keep talking while you code.
key_points: Paraphrase the question and clarify assumptions, input range and input format
Work through a small example to confirm you understand the problem
Explain at least one approach at a high level, with its trade-offs and its time and space complexity
Get the interviewer's agreement on the approach before starting to code
Keep explaining what you are doing while you code

questions.explanation: The Tech Interview Handbook rubric scores communication and problem solving as well as the code. A candidate who codes in silence gives the interviewer nothing to score on those two axes, even if the code works.

questions.prompt: You've just written the last line of your solution. What does the checklist say to do next?

choices.text: Say "done" straight away so the interviewer can move to the next question
Scan for mistakes, brainstorm edge cases with the interviewer, trace the code
Rewrite the solution in fewer lines to show fluency with the language
Ask the interviewer to run it and tell you whether it passes all of their tests

questions.explanation: After coding, the checklist says: scan your code for mistakes, brainstorm edge cases with the interviewer, step through the code with those cases, and restate the time and space complexity. It explicitly says not to announce straight away that you're done. The rubric's Testing axis rewards finding and fixing your own bugs.

questions.prompt:
The interviewer said the list may be empty. Stepping through this code with which input reveals a bug?

```python
def max_profit(prices):
    best = 0
    low = prices[0]
    for p in prices[1:]:
        low = min(low, p)
        best = max(best, p - low)
    return best
```
questions.explanation: `prices[0]` on an empty list raises `IndexError`. The others work: `[7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]` returns 5 (buy at 1, sell at 6), `[7, 6, 4, 3, 1]` returns 0, and `[2, 4, 1]` returns 2, because `best` keeps the earlier profit after `low` drops to 1. Edge cases like empty input are the ones to brainstorm before you say you're done.

sources.title: Built-in Exceptions - Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Python raises IndexError when a sequence subscript is out of range, so prices[0] on an empty list fails; the other inputs trace to 5, 0 and 2.

sources.title: Array cheatsheet for coding interviews | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The array cheatsheet lists an empty sequence as an array corner case.

choices.text: O(n), because each element is visited once
O(n log n), because `in` searches the list efficiently
O(n²), because `x in seen` scans the list
O(1) amortised, because `append` is amortised O(1)

questions.explanation: `x in seen` on a list is a linear scan, O(n). It runs once per element, so with no duplicates the total is 1 + 2 + … + n, which is O(n²). `append` is amortised O(1), but that doesn't change the cost of the scan. Making `seen` a `set` makes each membership test O(1) on average, and the loop O(n).

sources.title: TimeComplexity - Python Wiki
sources.claim: The Python wiki gives list membership (x in s) as O(n) and append as O(1) amortized, so n membership tests on a growing list are O(n^2) worst case.

questions.prompt: Your peer's feedback says: "Complexity analysis was shaky." State the time and space complexity of `has_duplicate` when `seen` is a `set`, and explain what "average case" means here.

model_answer.summary: Time is O(n) on average and space is O(n). Set lookups and inserts are O(1) on average because the set is a hash table, but they can be O(n) in the worst case when many hashes collide.
key_points: Each `x in seen` and `seen.add(x)` on a set is O(1) on average, so the loop is O(n) time on average
The set can hold up to n items, so extra space is O(n)
"Average" assumes a good hash function that makes collisions rare; the worst case per lookup is O(n)
State both time and space, and name the trade-off: the list version uses O(n²) time, and the set spends O(n) memory to get O(n) time

questions.explanation: The Python wiki's TimeComplexity page lists set membership as O(1) average and O(n) worst case, and list membership as O(n). Interviewers often probe what "average" means, and the answer is the hashing assumption.

sources.title: TimeComplexity - Python Wiki
sources.claim: The Python wiki lists set membership as O(1) average and O(n) worst case, and notes average-case times assume a hash function robust enough to make collisions uncommon.

questions.prompt: The Tech Interview Handbook says top companies score coding interviews on four axes. Which four?

choices.text: Speed, correctness, language trivia and culture fit
Communication, problem solving, technical competency and testing
Algorithm choice, code length, typing speed and confidence
Problem solving, system design, testing and leadership

questions.explanation: The handbook's rubric page lists communication, problem solving, technical competency and testing, and interviewers give a verdict such as Strong hire, Hire, No hire or Strong no hire. Speed and code length aren't axes: a slower, clearly explained, tested solution can score better than a fast silent one.

sources.title: How candidates are evaluated in coding interviews at top tech companies | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The handbook lists communication, problem solving, technical competency and testing as the axes, with overall bands of Strong hire, Hire, No hire and Strong no hire.

questions.prompt: You want written feedback from your peer that you can act on. Explain what you would ask them to write, using the four rubric axes.

model_answer.summary: Ask for a verdict and one or two specific things you did or didn't do on each axis: communication, problem solving, technical competency and testing. Then turn each weak axis into a drill for the next mock.
key_points: Name the four axes: communication, problem solving, technical competency, testing
Ask for specific behaviours on each axis (such as "didn't state space complexity" or "never tested an empty input"), not general impressions
Ask for an overall verdict on the Strong hire / Hire / No hire / Strong no hire scale
Turn each weak axis into one concrete practice item for the next mock

questions.explanation: Feedback tied to the rubric matches how real interviewers write up a candidate. The Tech Interview Handbook lists observable signals under each axis, such as asking clarifying questions, stating complexity accurately and handling corner cases, so your peer can check each one.

questions.prompt: Which opening behaviors help a peer follow a coding-mock solution? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Begin implementation while leaving every input assumption unstated.
Paraphrase the task and clarify ambiguous constraints.
Keep the approach private until the implementation is complete.
Work an example and explain an approach with complexity costs.
Agree on the approach before coding and continue explaining your work.

C: Incorrect: communication includes the planned approach and rationale. D: Correct: examples and cost analysis make the plan understandable. E: Correct: the interviewer should be able to follow the chosen solution.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe scanning n items with a Python seen set? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Expected constant-time membership makes the scan linear on average.
Set membership is guaranteed constant time even under severe hash collisions.
The set may require linear additional storage for distinct items.
A single set lookup can take linear time in the worst case.
Keeping all n distinct items in seen requires constant extra space.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: expected O(1) operations repeated n times give expected O(n) work. B: Incorrect: average-case guarantees depend on robust hashing. C: Correct: the set can grow to n entries. D: Correct: the Python complexity table lists O(n) worst-case membership. E: Incorrect: storage grows with the number of retained items.
